name: Ewa Kłobukowska
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic gold in the 4x100m relay (setting a world record) and bronze in the 100m at the 1964 Tokyo Olympics at age 18.
early_history_summary: Kłobukowska was a top European junior sprinter who won 100m and 4x100m relay golds at the 1964 European Junior Championships before the Olympics. She set her first world record in the 4x100m relay just a month before the Tokyo Games, then won Olympic gold and bronze at 18. She went on to set an individual world record in the 100m (11.1s) in 1965 and became European champion in 1966.
evidence_summary: Kłobukowska emerged from the Polish athletics system (Skra Warszawa club) to win Olympic gold at 18, setting world records in the relay. Her physical talent was exceptional — individual world record in the 100m at 19 and European champion at 20. No family background or financial advantage is documented in reviewed sources. Her career was cut short at 21 by a discredited gender verification test in 1967.
starting_point: Born in Warsaw, Poland; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Retired from sport after 1967; worked at an industrial equipment firm; as of 2025 is alive at age 79 and has received multiple Polish state honors including the Commander's Cross.

name: Kim Duk-koo
milestone_by_age_26: Won the OPBF (Orient and Pacific Boxing Federation) lightweight title in February 1982 and became the WBA's number 1 contender for the world lightweight championship at age 26.
early_history_summary: Kim was born into poverty in Gangwon Province, South Korea, and learned to fight on the streets. He started amateur boxing at age 17 in 1976 at Seoul's Tong-a Gymnasium, compiling a 29-4 amateur record. He turned professional in 1978, won the Korean lightweight title in December 1980, and won the OPBF title in February 1982 to become the WBA's top-ranked contender. He died from injuries sustained in a world title fight against Ray Mancini in November 1982.

name: Áron Szilágyi
milestone_by_age_26: Won team gold at the 2007 World Fencing Championships in Saint Petersburg at age 17, the first Hungarian gold in men's sabre since 1998, and was named Hungarian team of the year.

He was called up to the senior Hungarian national team as a cadet at 17 for the 2007 World Championships, where the team won gold. He made his Olympic debut at 18 in Beijing, won individual Olympic gold at 22 in London, and became the first male fencer to win three consecutive individual Olympic gold medals.

This mentor relationship and the Hungarian fencing pipeline — one of the world's strongest — propelled him to World Championship team gold at 17 and individual Olympic gold at 22. He became the first male fencer to win three consecutive individual Olympic golds, making him a tier-1 legend in the sport. No family financial advantage is documented.

She was one of only eight players to be part of all three Olympic gold campaigns and was inducted into the International Volleyball Hall of Fame in 2024.
